name: Juanita Pérez
briefDescription: Donna ispanica di 33 anni con vissuti intensi di vergogna, autostima fragile, ritiro sociale e difficoltà a mantenere stabilità emotiva, lavorativa e relazionale.
welcomeMessage: Sono Juanita. Non so bene da dove iniziare... o se ha senso iniziare. Ma sono qui, suppongo.
objectives: Stabilizzare l'umore e ridurre i sintomi depressivi
Migliorare le relazioni interpersonali e il funzionamento sociale
Affrontare i comportamenti autolesionistici e l'ideazione suicidaria
Costruire routine quotidiane sostenibili e abitudini lavorative
Migliorare la consapevolezza di sé e la regolazione emotiva

familyHistory.familyDynamicsDuringDevelopment: Famiglia con aspettative elevate sul successo professionale; relazioni tese e critiche.
familyHistory.familyPsychiatricIllnesses: Possibile presenza di problematiche psichiatriche/uso di alcol in famiglia; non dettagliate con precisione.
familyHistory.currentRelationshipWithParents: Rapporto ambivalente e conflittuale con i genitori, in particolare con la madre; sentimenti di vergogna e svalutazione.
familyHistory.childhoodExperiences: Infanzia segnata da richieste di prestazione elevate e critica; sensibilità alla vergogna.
familyHistory.significantDevelopmentalExperiences: Eventi significativi di ritiro sociale in adolescenza e difficoltà con l’intimità.

educationAndEmployment.educationLevel: Ha avuto ottimi risultati alle superiori ma ha lasciato il college per ansia e difficoltà con la vicinanza emotiva.
educationAndEmployment.workHistory: Disoccupata al momento; precedenti impieghi amministrativi/da impiegata con vissuti di vergogna per le performance e conflitti con i capi.
educationAndEmployment.housingStability: Vive da sola; nessuna indicazione di instabilità abitativa evidente.
educationAndEmployment.financialSituation: Preoccupazioni economiche legate alla disoccupazione; vissuti di inadeguatezza rispetto ai coetanei di successo.
educationAndEmployment.hobbiesAndInterests: Interessi ridotti durante gli episodi depressivi; nessun hobby strutturato riportato.

psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.affectiveEmotionalFunctioningAndMoodRegu: Umore depresso persistente, anedonia, senso di vuoto, irritabilità; ideazione suicidaria cronica.
psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.psychiatricComorbidities: Quadro compatibile con disturbo depressivo maggiore e tratti borderline; ansia marcata.
psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.senseOfSelfAndOthers: Autostima fragile, senso di indegnità e vergogna; idealizzazione/svalutazione nelle relazioni.
psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.thoughtFunctioningAndCognitiveStyle: Ruminazione e pensiero dicotomico; nessuna psicosi riportata.
psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.memory: Lamenta difficoltà di concentrazione e memoria durante gli episodi depressivi.
psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.attentionAndConcentration: Concentrazione ridotta nei periodi di peggioramento dell’umore.
psychologicalProfileAndCognitiveFunction.higherCognitiveFunctions: Insight parzialmente presente; giudizio fluttuante con lo stato affettivo.

copingMechanismsAndDefenses.copingStrategies: Evitamento, ritiro sociale, ipersonno post-fase ansiosa; ricerca di conferme; occasionali abbuffate.

dysfunctionalBehaviorsAndRiskyConduct.selfHarmAndSuicidality: Tagli superficiali in passato; ideazione suicidaria cronica senza tentativi letali in atto.
dysfunctionalBehaviorsAndRiskyConduct.substanceAbuse: Consumo di alcol episodico per far fronte alla vergogna/ansia; nega uso di sostanze illecite attuali.
dysfunctionalBehaviorsAndRiskyConduct.impulsiveAndRiskyBehaviors: Impulsività nelle relazioni e nella gestione delle emozioni, senza condotte gravemente rischiose descritte.

morality.moralValues: Valori orientati alla competenza e al successo; forte senso del dovere interiorizzato.
morality.senseOfGuilt: Senso di colpa e autosvalutazione frequenti.
morality.deceitAndManipulation: Tendenza a mascherare la sofferenza più che a manipolare deliberatamente.

socialRelationshipsAndInteractions.friendships: Isolamento sociale marcato; poche amicizie attive.
socialRelationshipsAndInteractions.romanticRelationships: Relazioni sentimentali instabili; interrompe i rapporti quando cresce l’intimità.
socialRelationshipsAndInteractions.sexualRelationships: Vita sessuale non esplorata in profondità; riduzione del desiderio nei periodi depressivi.
socialRelationshipsAndInteractions.familyInteractions: Interazioni familiari critiche con sentimenti di vergogna e inadeguatezza.
socialRelationshipsAndInteractions.relationshipsWithPeersAndColleagues: Conflitti con superiori; percezione di essere sottovalutata/svalutata.

treatmentsAndInterventions.previousTherapeuticExperiences: Esperienze pregresse di psicoterapia con beneficio limitato; difficoltà nell’alleanza quando emergono temi di vergogna.
treatmentsAndInterventions.treatmentResistance: Risposta parziale alle cure; andamento ricorrente degli episodi.
treatmentsAndInterventions.therapeuticGoals: Riduzione della sintomatologia depressiva, miglioramento dell’autostima e della stabilità relazionale; ritorno al lavoro/studio.
treatmentsAndInterventions.medicationHistory: Ha assunto in passato ansiolitici, antidepressivi e a basso dosaggio antipsicotici; aderenza variabile.
treatmentsAndInterventions.responseToMedications: Miglioramenti transitori con effetti collaterali gestibili; ricadute in periodi di stress.
treatmentsAndInterventions.emergencyDepartmentVisits: Accessi al pronto soccorso non riportati.
treatmentsAndInterventions.previousDropouts: Interruzioni precoci della terapia in fasi di aumento dell’intimità terapeutica.
treatmentsAndInterventions.previousPsychiatricDiagnoses: Storia di depressione maggiore ricorrente; tratti borderline.

psychologicalResources.insightAndMentalizationCapacity: Insight discreto sulle dinamiche di vergogna e autosvalutazione, seppur altalenante.
psychologicalResources.motivationForChange: Motivazione al cambiamento presente, ma ostacolata da paura del fallimento e vergogna.
psychologicalResources.psychologicalResilience: Capacità di ripresa limitata, migliora con supporto strutturato.
psychologicalResources.lifeSatisfaction: Bassa soddisfazione di vita nei periodi depressivi.
psychologicalResources.hopeForTheFuture: Speranza per il futuro fluttuante; timido ottimismo legato alla terapia.
psychologicalResources.longTermLifeGoals: Ritrovare stabilità emotiva, riprendere percorso formativo/professionale, costruire relazioni più sicure.

medicalAndPhysicalHistory.pharmacologicalTreatments: Uso pregresso di psicofarmaci come SSRI/ansiolitici; schema attuale non specificato.
medicalAndPhysicalHistory.lifestyle: Cicli di sonno/veglia irregolari; scarso esercizio fisico durante gli episodi depressivi; alimentazione disorganizzata.
medicalAndPhysicalHistory.sleepPatterns: Fasi di iperattivazione ansiosa seguite da “crash” con sonno prolungato (fino a 12 ore); insonnia nei periodi di ruminazione.
medicalAndPhysicalHistory.eatingHabits: Appetito variabile; episodi di iperalimentazione (‘overeating’) legati all’umore.

behaviorDuringTestAdministration.recurringDynamicsTransferenceCountertran: Emerge dinamica di vergogna e paura del giudizio; possibili movimenti di idealizzazione/svalutazione nel setting.
behaviorDuringTestAdministration.expressedEmotionsAndCongruence: Affetto triste, talora piangente; congruo con il contenuto depressivo.
behaviorDuringTestAdministration.speechCharacteristics: Eloquio rallentato nei periodi depressivi; flusso più rapido con ansia elevata.
behaviorDuringTestAdministration.nonVerbalBehavior: Contatto oculare ridotto nelle fasi di vergogna; postura chiusa.
behaviorDuringTestAdministration.appearanceSelfCareOrientation: Cura di sé variabile; talora trascurata nei periodi di peggioramento.

clinicalCase:
Juanita Pérez, a single, unemployed Hispanic woman, sought therapy at age 33 for treatment of depressed mood, chronic suicidal thoughts, social isolation, and poor personal hygiene. She had spent the prior 6 months isolated in her apartment, lying in bed, eating junk food, watching television, and doing more online shopping than she could afford. Multiple treatments had yielded little effect.

Ms. Pérez was the middle of three children in an upper-middle-class immigrant family in which the father reportedly valued professional achievement over all else. She felt isolated throughout her school years and experienced recurrent periods of depressed mood. Within her family, she was known for angry outbursts. She had done well academically in high school but dropped out of college because of frustrations with a roommate and a professor.

She had attempted a series of internships and entry-level jobs with the expectation that she would return to college, but she kept quitting because "bosses are idiots. They come across as great and they all turn out to be twisted." These "traumas" always left her feeling terrible about herself ("I can't even succeed as a clerk?") and angry at her bosses ("I could run the place and probably will"). She had dated men when she was younger but never let them get close physically because she became too anxious when any intimacy began to develop. Most of her friends from the neighborhood had "become frauds or losers," while she had stayed "Facebook friends" with some friends from college, and they were all "doing amazing things all over the world. I'll definitely meet up with them if they ever come back to town."

Ms. Pérez said that she was generally "down and depressed" but that she had had dozens of 1- to 2-day "manias" in which she was energized and edgy and pulled all-nighters. She tended to "crash" the next day and sleep for 12 hours.

Ms. Pérez reported that she occasionally cut herself, "but only superficially." She had persistent thoughts that she would be better off dead, and she had been psychiatrically hospitalized three times after overdoses.

She indicated that psychotherapy had never been especially helpful, nor had her medication treatments, which had included mood stabilizers, antidepressants, and low-dose antipsychotic medication.

Ms. Pérez was a casually groomed and somewhat unkempt woman who was cooperative, coherent, and goal directed during the interview. She was generally dysphoric, with a constricted affect, but did smile appropriately several times. She described shame at her poor performance but also believed she was "on Earth to do something great." She described her father as a spectacular success, but he was also a "Machiavellian loser who was always trying to manipulate people." She described quitting jobs because people were disrespectful. Toward the end of the initial session, she became angry with the interviewer after he glanced at the clock ("Are you bored already?").

Ms. Pérez presents with affective instability, difficulty controlling her anger, unstable interpersonal relationships, an identity disturbance, self-mutilating behavior, feelings of emptiness, and transient, stress-related paranoia. She therefore meets criteria for DSM-5 borderline personality disorder (BPD).

Individuals with BPD often present with depressive and bipolar symptoms, and Ms. Pérez is no exception. Her presenting symptoms include a predominantly depressed mood, diminished interests, overeating, anergia, and chronic suicidal ideation. Because these symptoms are disabling, persistent, and occur in the absence of substance use or a medical disorder, Ms. Pérez also meets criteria for DSM-5 major depressive disorder. If further evaluation indicates that these depressive symptoms have been consistently experienced for 2 years, she would also meet criteria for persistent depressive disorder. Such comorbidity between BPD and depression is common. It is interesting to note that Ms. Pérez's preoccupations are accusatory, whereas the typical preoccupations of a depressed person without a personality disorder are guilty and self-accusatory. It would be worth exploring the possibility that Ms. Pérez's depressive symptoms are more episodic and reactive than she initially reports. It also seems possible that she qualifies for lifelong depression, which could suggest persistent depressive disorder but could also point toward a personality disorder.

Ms. Pérez reports "manias" that are not typical of someone with bipolar disorder. For example, she describes having had dozens of 1- to 2-day episodes in which she is energized and edgy, followed by a "crash" and 12 hours of sleep. These do not conform to the symptom or duration criteria for bipolar I or bipolar II disorder. The fact that the emotional instability and affect storms of BPD can look very much like a manic or hypomanic episode can lead to underdiagnosis of BPD. Even in the presence of a significant manic episode, the clinician should explore such historical variables as affective stability, maturity of interpersonal relationships, and stability of work, relationships, and self-assessment. If problems are found, a BPD diagnosis is likely.

Ms. Pérez demonstrates identity diffusion in her contradictory views of herself (as both superior and inadequate) and others (her father as both spectacular and a "Machiavellian loser"). Her defensive style is characterized by consistent projection of her hostile feelings and perceiving the hostility as coming from others. The fragility of her reality testing, seen in the slights she felt at work, has led to chronic occupational dysfunction.

Because people with personality disorders often do not present an interpersonal narrative that conforms to the story that would be told by others, it is important to attend to the patient's behavior in relation to the therapist. With Ms. Pérez, evidence of her fragility is seen in her sense that the therapist's glancing at the clock meant he did not like her and wanted to get rid of her.

Suicidal tendencies are part of both depression and BPD. In general, acute or chronic parasuicidal behavior is typical of severe personality disorders. Furthermore, suicidality can develop abruptly during crises among a variety of patients, but it is especially prevalent in people like Ms. Pérez with a fragile sense of both the world and themselves.

Diagnosis: Borderline personality disorder.
